articles.title: EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers
articles.summary:
Click to expand Image
          



  
        
  

        
                      
      
        
              A readymade garment worker in a green factory in Savar, Bangladesh, on April 9, 2025.
                    © 2025 Ahmed Salahuddin/NurPhoto via Getty Images
          
    


  
(Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today. In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.“Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”The groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part. An estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.Academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.The civil society groups said that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.Companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.The EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages. “Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé said. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”
articles.content:
Click to expand Image A readymade garment worker in a green factory in Savar, Bangladesh, on April 9, 2025. © 2025 Ahmed Salahuddin/NurPhoto via Getty Images

(Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today.

In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

“Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”

The groups propose concrete steps for companies to prepare, deliver and assess their remediation obligations. The report comes as the European Union prepares to enforce its Forced Labour Regulation, which will ban products made with forced labor from the EU market across all sectors and stages of production beginning on December 14, 2027. Under the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, companies in its scope will also have a legal duty to remedy harm they cause, completely or in part.

An estimated 17.3 million people were in situations of forced labor in the private economy in 2022, according to global estimates by the International Labour Organization (ILO), Walk Free, and the International Organization for Migration. The number of victims increased by 8 percent between 2016 and 2021. The ILO estimates that forced labor in the private economy generates US$63.9 billion in illegal profits every year.

Academics and experts found that forced labor is rarely only the result of a few bad actors, but is rooted in poverty, discrimination, weak labor protections, and restrictive migration regimes. Migrant workers face heightened risks, including recruitment fees that lead to debt bondage, deceptive recruitment practices, and visas tied to a single employer. Fear of deportation and retaliation often keeps victims from seeking redress.

The civil society groups said that companies should put in place remediation measures that restore as much as possible the situation for workers if the abuse had not occurred. This would require the cessation of the abuse, restitution, rehabilitation, compensation, apologies, and guarantees of non-repetition. Companies should also ensure that workers and their representatives can identify abuses through grievance mechanisms they trust, define remedies, and assess whether they have been delivered to their satisfaction, the groups said. At all times, affected workers should be protected from retaliation.

Companies should treat remediation as part of their human rights due diligence, not as a one-off response to a scandal, the groups said. Their responsibility should reflect their involvement in failing to prevent or meaningfully address the harm. Companies should not “cut and run” from suppliers when and where labor abuses, including forced labor, is found, as this can leave workers worse off. Instead, the groups said, companies should fairly agree on how to address and share remediation costs.

To prevent forced labor from occurring and recurring, companies should examine structural causes such as poverty, discrimination and impairments to freedom of association but also how their own purchasing practices may drive it. They should pay to cover the cost of decent working conditions and living wages. The groups point to worker-driven models, such as the Fair Food Program in US agriculture and the Dindigul Agreement in India’s textile sector, as evidence of good practices.

The EU and its member states should ensure that the competent authorities empowered to enforce the Forced Labour Regulation assess whether effective remediation has actually delivered for workers, including through workers’ own accounts and evidence of compensation paid. They should also ensure that, regardless of their migration status, workers can at least access support, file complaints, and recover unpaid wages.

“Workers know best what they have lost and what it will take to rebuild their lives,” de Rengervé said. “Companies and EU authorities should listen to affected workers and measure the efficiency of remediation by what workers receive and whether they completely remediate the harm suffered.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant and concrete initiative by the EU and civil society groups to ensure companies provide effective remedies to workers subjected to forced labor, addressing a major human rights abuse affecting millions globally. It outlines specific steps and legal frameworks aimed at restoring workers' rights and dignity, with broad societal impact and detailed context.
articles.personality_title: EU and groups call for real help to workers trapped in forced labor
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Forced labor affects millions worldwide, often hidden in supply chains where workers face debt, threats, and unfair conditions. The European Union is preparing new rules to stop products made with forced labor from entering its market by the end of 2027.

**What happened** – Human Rights Watch, together with civil society groups and trade unions, released a report urging companies to give full support and fair compensation to workers caught in forced labor. They outlined clear steps companies should take to fix harm, such as paying wages owed, returning documents, and protecting workers from punishment for speaking up.

**Impact** – This approach focuses on helping workers directly, not just removing products from shelves. It highlights that fixing forced labor means restoring workers’ dignity and rights, not abandoning them. The report also points out how forced labor is linked to poverty, migration rules, and unfair business practices, offering examples of successful worker-led programs.

**What's next step** – The EU will start enforcing its Forced Labour Regulation in December 2027, making it illegal to sell goods made with forced labor. Companies covered by new rules must also actively fix harms they cause. Authorities will check if workers actually receive help and compensation, ensuring their voices guide the process.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New EU rules and expert guidance aim to ensure companies fully support workers harmed by forced labor, focusing on real remedies that restore their rights and lives.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’UE et des groupes demandent une aide réelle aux travailleurs victimes du travail forcé
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le travail forcé touche des millions de personnes dans le monde, souvent caché dans les chaînes d'approvisionnement où les travailleurs subissent dettes, menaces et conditions injustes. L’Union européenne prépare de nouvelles règles pour interdire les produits issus du travail forcé sur son marché d’ici fin 2027.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Human Rights Watch, avec des organisations de la société civile et des syndicats, a publié un rapport demandant aux entreprises d’apporter un soutien complet et une compensation juste aux travailleurs victimes de travail forcé. Ils ont décrit des étapes claires pour réparer les torts, comme payer les salaires dus, rendre les documents et protéger les travailleurs contre les représailles.

**Impact** – Cette approche se concentre sur l’aide directe aux travailleurs, et pas seulement sur le retrait des produits. Elle montre que réparer le travail forcé, c’est redonner dignité et droits aux travailleurs, pas les abandonner. Le rapport souligne aussi que le travail forcé est lié à la pauvreté, aux règles migratoires et aux pratiques commerciales injustes, en citant des exemples de programmes réussis dirigés par les travailleurs.

**Prochaine étape** – L’UE appliquera son règlement sur le travail forcé en décembre 2027, rendant illégal la vente de produits issus du travail forcé. Les entreprises concernées devront aussi réparer activement les préjudices qu’elles causent. Les autorités vérifieront que les travailleurs reçoivent réellement de l’aide et des compensations, en tenant compte de leurs témoignages.

**Message clé en une phrase** – De nouvelles règles européennes et des recommandations d’experts visent à garantir que les entreprises soutiennent pleinement les travailleurs victimes de travail forcé, en réparant réellement leurs droits et leur vie.
articles.personality_title_es: La UE y grupos exigen ayuda real a trabajadores atrapados en trabajo forzoso
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El trabajo forzoso afecta a millones en todo el mundo, a menudo oculto en cadenas de suministro donde los trabajadores enfrentan deudas, amenazas y condiciones injustas. La Unión Europea prepara nuevas reglas para prohibir productos hechos con trabajo forzoso en su mercado para finales de 2027.

**Qué pasó** – Human Rights Watch, junto con grupos civiles y sindicatos, lanzó un informe que insta a las empresas a brindar apoyo completo y compensación justa a los trabajadores atrapados en trabajo forzoso. Detallaron pasos claros para reparar daños, como pagar salarios adeudados, devolver documentos y proteger a los trabajadores de represalias.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque se centra en ayudar directamente a los trabajadores, no solo en retirar productos de las tiendas. Destaca que reparar el trabajo forzoso significa restaurar la dignidad y los derechos de los trabajadores, no abandonarlos. El informe también señala que el trabajo forzoso está ligado a la pobreza, las normas migratorias y prácticas comerciales injustas, y menciona ejemplos de programas exitosos dirigidos por los propios trabajadores.

**Próximo paso** – La UE comenzará a aplicar su Regulación sobre Trabajo Forzoso en diciembre de 2027, prohibiendo la venta de productos fabricados con trabajo forzoso. Las empresas bajo estas normas deberán reparar activamente los daños causados. Las autoridades evaluarán si los trabajadores realmente reciben ayuda y compensación, tomando en cuenta sus testimonios.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Nuevas reglas de la UE y orientación experta buscan garantizar que las empresas apoyen plenamente a los trabajadores afectados por trabajo forzoso, enfocándose en remedios reales que restauren sus derechos y vidas.

articles.title: Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit
articles.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has published his review of the personal independence payment (Pip), along with recommended changes.
articles.content:
First the short term.

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Then the long term.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a government review recommending significant improvements to the Personal Independence Payment system for disabled people, aiming to make the process faster, fairer, and less stressful, which positively impacts a broad and vulnerable population.
articles.personality_title: New review aims to make disability benefit faster and fairer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is a benefit in the UK that helps disabled people with extra costs caused by their condition. Recently, the government asked Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, to review how PIP works and suggest improvements.

**What happened** – Sir Stephen Timms published his review with several recommendations. For people with terminal illnesses or severe, stable conditions, he suggests a fast-track process that avoids lengthy assessments. For everyone else, the review proposes a clearer and fairer initial assessment to understand how their disability affects daily life and what support they need. The review also recommends optional support services and a new way to ask about extra costs without complicated paperwork. Lastly, it suggests reviewing the rule that stops payments if someone stays in hospital for more than 28 days.

**Impact** – These changes could make it easier and less stressful for disabled people to get the support they need. Fast-tracking the most serious cases means quicker help when time is limited. Updating assessments and support options can make sure people receive the right amount of money and services. Changing the hospital rule may reduce delays and stress during hospital stays.

**What's next step** – The government will consider these recommendations and decide which to put into action. If adopted, the PIP system will change to better meet the needs of disabled people, possibly starting with the fast-track process and new assessment questions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new review proposes faster and fairer ways to help disabled people get the support they need through the Personal Independence Payment system.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle revue vise à rendre l'allocation pour handicapés plus rapide et plus juste
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Prestation d'Indépendance Personnelle (PIP) est une aide au Royaume-Uni pour les personnes handicapées, afin de couvrir les coûts supplémentaires liés à leur condition. Récemment, le gouvernement a demandé à Sir Stephen Timms, ministre chargé du handicap, de revoir le fonctionnement de la PIP et de proposer des améliorations.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Sir Stephen Timms a publié son rapport avec plusieurs recommandations. Pour les personnes atteintes de maladies en phase terminale ou de conditions graves et stables, il propose un processus accéléré évitant des évaluations longues. Pour les autres, le rapport suggère une évaluation initiale plus claire et équitable pour comprendre comment le handicap affecte la vie quotidienne et les besoins de soutien. Le rapport recommande aussi des services de soutien optionnels et une nouvelle façon de poser des questions sur les coûts supplémentaires sans formalités compliquées. Enfin, il propose de revoir la règle qui suspend les paiements si une personne reste plus de 28 jours à l'hôpital.

**Impact** – Ces changements pourraient faciliter et rendre moins stressant l'accès au soutien pour les personnes handicapées. L'accélération des cas les plus graves permet une aide plus rapide quand le temps est compté. La mise à jour des évaluations et des options de soutien peut garantir que chacun reçoive la bonne somme d'argent et services. Modifier la règle sur l'hospitalisation pourrait réduire les retards et le stress lors des séjours à l'hôpital.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement va examiner ces recommandations et décider lesquelles appliquer. Si elles sont adoptées, le système PIP évoluera pour mieux répondre aux besoins des personnes handicapées, probablement en commençant par le processus accéléré et les nouvelles questions d'évaluation.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle revue propose des moyens plus rapides et plus justes pour aider les personnes handicapées à obtenir le soutien nécessaire via la prestation d'indépendance personnelle.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva revisión busca hacer el beneficio por discapacidad más rápido y justo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Pago de Independencia Personal (PIP) es un beneficio en el Reino Unido que ayuda a las personas con discapacidad a cubrir los costos extra causados por su condición. Recientemente, el gobierno pidió al ministro de discapacidad, Sir Stephen Timms, que revisara cómo funciona el PIP y propusiera mejoras.

**Qué pasó** – Sir Stephen Timms publicó su revisión con varias recomendaciones. Para las personas con enfermedades terminales o condiciones graves y estables, sugiere un proceso rápido que evite evaluaciones largas. Para los demás, la revisión propone una evaluación inicial más clara y justa para entender cómo la discapacidad afecta la vida diaria y qué apoyo necesitan. También recomienda servicios de apoyo opcionales y una nueva forma de preguntar sobre costos extra sin papeleo complicado. Por último, sugiere revisar la regla que suspende los pagos si alguien permanece más de 28 días en el hospital.

**Impacto** – Estos cambios podrían facilitar y hacer menos estresante que las personas con discapacidad reciban el apoyo que necesitan. El proceso rápido para casos graves significa ayuda más pronta cuando el tiempo es limitado. Actualizar las evaluaciones y opciones de apoyo puede asegurar que las personas reciban la cantidad correcta de dinero y servicios. Cambiar la regla del hospital podría reducir retrasos y estrés durante las estancias hospitalarias.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno considerará estas recomendaciones y decidirá cuáles implementar. Si se adoptan, el sistema PIP cambiará para atender mejor las necesidades de las personas con discapacidad, posiblemente comenzando con el proceso rápido y las nuevas preguntas de evaluación.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Una nueva revisión propone formas más rápidas y justas para ayudar a las personas con discapacidad a obtener el apoyo que necesitan a través del sistema de Pago de Independencia Personal.

articles.title: Colombia: Guterres urges renewed commitment to landmark peace deal
articles.summary: UN Secretary-General António Guterres has commended Colombia for progress achieved in the decade since a landmark accord known as the Final Peace Agreement ended more than 50 years of insurgency but stressed the need to fully implement its provisions.
articles.content:
“Ten years ago, the people of Colombia took an inspiring step toward peace,” his Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said in a statement on Tuesday.

The Final Peace Agreement was signed by the Government and FARC-EP rebels in the capital, Bogotá, on 24 November 2016.

The Secretary-General expressed deep appreciation for all that has been achieved to chart a more peaceful, inclusive and secure future for Colombians.

Step up commitment

With five years remaining in the timeframe for implementation, he encouraged redoubled commitment to key processes initiated under the Agreement.

They include peacefully reintegrating former combatants into society, expanding development and State presence to marginalised territories and communities, and guaranteeing victims’ rights through the transitional justice system.

Meanwhile, the Secretary-General remains deeply concerned about the violence plaguing regions still affected by conflict, underscoring that the peace deal “remains a valuable instrument at the disposal of Colombia’s authorities as they seek today to bring greater security and development to these territories.”

Mr. Guterres commended the dedication and perseverance of the parties, institutions, civil society and the Colombian people in advancing peace, and reaffirmed UN commitment to continue accompanying these efforts.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the significant progress and ongoing efforts to implement a landmark peace agreement in Colombia that ended decades of conflict, which has broad societal impact by promoting peace, security, and justice for many people. It highlights a meaningful, large-scale positive change with sufficient context about the peace process and its goals.
articles.personality_title: Colombia marks 10 years of peace agreement with progress and renewed efforts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Colombia experienced more than 50 years of conflict between the government and the FARC-EP rebel group. In 2016, they signed the Final Peace Agreement to end the fighting and start building peace.

**What happened** – On the 10th anniversary of the peace deal, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres praised Colombia for the progress made. He reminded everyone that there are still important parts of the agreement to complete, like helping former fighters return to normal life, improving conditions in poor regions, and supporting victims through justice processes.

**Impact** – This agreement is important because it has helped many Colombians live more peacefully and safely after decades of violence. The ongoing work aims to make sure no one is left behind, especially in areas that were most affected by the conflict.

**What's next step** – The next five years are crucial for finishing what the peace deal promises. Colombia’s leaders, communities, and the UN will continue working together to support development, security, and justice across the country.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Colombia is building on a decade of peace progress by focusing on fully carrying out a landmark agreement that ended decades of conflict.
articles.personality_title_fr: Colombie : dix ans après l’accord de paix, des progrès et un engagement renouvelé
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Colombie a connu plus de 50 ans de conflit entre le gouvernement et le groupe rebelle FARC-EP. En 2016, ils ont signé l’Accord final de paix pour mettre fin aux combats et commencer à construire la paix.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pour le 10e anniversaire de cet accord, le Secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a salué les progrès accomplis en Colombie. Il a rappelé que certaines parties importantes de l’accord restent à mettre en œuvre, comme la réintégration des anciens combattants, l’amélioration des conditions dans les régions défavorisées et l’accompagnement des victimes par la justice.

**Impact** – Cet accord est important car il a permis à de nombreux Colombiens de vivre plus paisiblement après des décennies de violence. Les efforts en cours visent à ne laisser personne de côté, surtout dans les zones les plus touchées par le conflit.

**Prochaine étape** – Les cinq prochaines années sont essentielles pour réaliser pleinement les promesses de l’accord. Les dirigeants colombiens, les communautés et l’ONU continueront à travailler ensemble pour soutenir le développement, la sécurité et la justice dans tout le pays.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La Colombie poursuit ses progrès vers la paix en se concentrant sur la mise en œuvre complète d’un accord historique qui a mis fin à des décennies de conflit.
articles.personality_title_es: Colombia celebra 10 años del acuerdo de paz con avances y compromiso renovado
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Colombia vivió más de 50 años de conflicto entre el gobierno y el grupo rebelde FARC-EP. En 2016 firmaron el Acuerdo Final de Paz para terminar la lucha y comenzar a construir la paz.

**Qué pasó** – En el décimo aniversario del acuerdo, el Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, elogió los avances hechos en Colombia. Recordó que aún quedan partes importantes por cumplir, como ayudar a los excombatientes a reintegrarse, mejorar las condiciones en zonas pobres y apoyar a las víctimas mediante la justicia.

**Impacto** – Este acuerdo es importante porque ha ayudado a muchos colombianos a vivir con más paz y seguridad después de años de violencia. El trabajo continúa para asegurar que nadie quede atrás, especialmente en las áreas más afectadas por el conflicto.

**Próximo paso** – Los próximos cinco años son clave para completar lo que promete el acuerdo. Los líderes, comunidades y la ONU seguirán trabajando juntos para apoyar el desarrollo, la seguridad y la justicia en todo el país.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Colombia avanza en la construcción de la paz al enfocarse en cumplir completamente un acuerdo histórico que puso fin a décadas de conflicto.

articles.title: Prince William meets Burnham on first Downing Street visit
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales is meeting Andy Burnham with homelessness expected to be among the topics.
articles.content:
Burnham has a weekly meeting with the prince's father, the King, and they are said to have developed a friendly relationship.

By convention, the Prince of Wales is meant to meet the prime minister once a year, but not necessarily at Downing Street. He met Sir Keir Starmer last year at Kensington Palace.

Prince William's appearance on a chilly morning will be seen as another step in his apprenticeship as a future king and head of state.

And it's expected that next year the prince will be carrying out more diplomatic visits at the request of the government.

The two men have a shared interest in addressing homelessness, which is expected to be among the topics under discussion.

Prince William has his Homewards project, which is testing ideas to reduce homelessness in six areas of the UK.

Burnham has pledged to give rough sleepers in England support to get off the streets by Christmas.

The prince and Andy Burnham have been active supporters of the Big Issue magazine which supports the homeless.

Both of the men have a reputation for being relaxed communicators in public, with Prince William recently getting plaudits for his unpompous appearance on the Graham Norton Show.

It's a relatively rare sight to see a royal in the prime minister's domain. The late Queen Elizabeth II visited in 1985 to commemorate the 250th anniversary of Downing Street and was here in 2012, when David Cameron was prime minister.

But there were no royal visitors during the intervening years, when Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer were prime ministers.

The then Prince Charles and Princess Diana visited 10 Downing Street in November 1989, for a dinner hosted by then then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a meaningful meeting between Prince William and Andy Burnham focused on addressing homelessness, a significant social issue affecting many people. The involvement of high-profile figures and ongoing projects like Homewards and commitments to support rough sleepers demonstrate tangible efforts to improve lives on a broad scale. The story is focused and provides sufficient context about the collaboration and its potential impact.
articles.personality_title: Prince William meets mayor to discuss helping homeless people
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Prince William, known as the Prince of Wales, usually meets the prime minister once a year but not always at Downing Street. This visit is special because royals rarely come to the prime minister’s office.

**What happened** – On a cold morning, Prince William met Andy Burnham, the Mayor of Greater Manchester, at Downing Street. They talked about homelessness and ways to help people without homes. Both have worked on projects to support homeless people, like Prince William’s Homewards project and Burnham’s promise to help rough sleepers by Christmas.
